Circle Center By Ruler

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Drag the dots to move two crossing circles and watch their straight lines point to the middle of one circle.
How to play: Drag M, N, A or B' with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claims to see what never changes.
Look for the math

Steinhaus asked for the centre of a circle using only a ruler, when a second circle crossing it is available. Drag the points and watch the lines: two lengths stay equal, and two crossings line up with the centre.

Two circles and four ruler lines

The circles meet at M and N. A sits on the first circle and B' on the second. The line AM meets the second circle again at B; the line BN meets the first circle again at C. Starting from B' instead gives A' and C' on the first circle. Only straight lines are drawn, yet the picture already hides the centre.

Why the two short chords match

The four marked angles ∠AMA', ∠CNC', ∠BMB' and ∠BNB' stand on chords of the same two circles. An inscribed angle standing on one chord has the same sine wherever its vertex sits on the circle. Angles from opposite arcs add to 180°, so the applet's "equal angles" are equal or supplementary in the ordinary 0–180° sense; their sines are always the same. The logic test checks those sines on thousands of diagrams. A chord of radius R cut by an inscribed angle θ has length 2·R·sin(θ), so AA' = CC'.

Lengths that do not move

Add arc AC' to the equal arcs AA' and CC' and you get another equal pair: arcs AC and A'C', so their chords match too. The test confirms AC = A'C' both as B' travels around its circle and as A travels around the first circle, with the two circles held fixed; a different second circle gives a different length. That is the second result on the original page: the length of AC does not depend on where B sits on its circle.

The diameter through P and Q

Let P = AC ∩ A'C' and Q = AA' ∩ CC'. The page says these two points lie on the diameter of the first circle perpendicular to AC' (or A'C'). The test measures the offset of O, P and Q from one straight line on thousands of diagrams and finds it at machine precision. When A' falls onto A, the lines AA' and CC' become the tangents at A and C: Q is then checked against the diameter perpendicular to chord AC instead, because P is the crossing of two nearly identical lines and cannot be located reliably. Two such diameters meet at the centre O, which is what the ruler-only construction wants.

Try Show equal angles, then drag B' close to B: the four marks stay the same size even as the lines sweep across the picture.
